### e)  Differential Abundance Analysis {.tabset}

Differential abundance was tested with <span class="go-tip" tabindex="0">DESeq2<span class="go-tiptext"><b>DESeq2</b> models raw read counts with a negative binomial distribution, normalizes samples with size factors, and compares groups with a Wald test. The x-axis is the log2 fold change. DESeq2 is usually the most sensitive of the three methods. It does not account for the compositional nature of microbiome data, and with small groups or sparse features a few samples can drive a significant result.</span></span>, <span class="go-tip" tabindex="0">ALDEx2<span class="go-tiptext"><b>ALDEx2</b> converts counts to centered log-ratios (CLR) over 128 Monte Carlo draws from a Dirichlet distribution, so the uncertainty of low counts is carried into the test. The test depends on the design. Without covariates, ALDEx2 runs its t-test option, which computes Welch's t-test and the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and the report uses the Wilcoxon p-value. With covariates, it fits a generalized linear model (GLM) instead. The plot title reads "aldex2-t-test" in both cases. The x-axis is the difference in CLR values between groups, or the GLM coefficient when covariates are included. ALDEx2 is conservative and usually reports the fewest significant features.</span></span>, and <span class="go-tip" tabindex="0">ANCOM-BC2<span class="go-tiptext"><b>ANCOM-BC2</b> fits a log-linear model that estimates and removes sample-specific sampling bias. Features present in fewer than 10% of samples are excluded, and features absent from one group are handled as structural zeros. The x-axis is the natural-log fold change. ANCOM-BC2 controls false discoveries well but has limited power in small studies.</span></span>, comparing each group with the reference group where the comparison was possible. Hover over a method name or <span class="go-tip" tabindex="0">Reading the results<span class="go-tiptext"><b>Reading the results</b><span class="go-tipitem">Point colors show the group in which a feature is higher; grey points are not significant.</span><span class="go-tipitem">Open circles mark p &lt; 0.05 without correction for multiple testing; when hundreds of features are tested, about 5% reach this by chance. Closed circles mark FDR-adjusted p &lt; 0.05.</span><span class="go-tipitem">All three methods estimate changes in relative abundance, not absolute abundance. A large increase in one taxon can make other taxa appear lower.</span><span class="go-tipitem">The methods rest on different assumptions and often disagree. A feature that is significant in two or three methods is more reliable than one found by a single method.</span><span class="go-tipitem">Effect sizes are on a different scale in each plot and cannot be compared across the three methods.</span><span class="go-tipitem">Small or unequal groups limit statistical power. Finding no significant feature does not show that the groups are the same.</span><span class="go-tipitem">Check how common and how abundant each significant feature is. A large fold change in a feature found in only a few samples is weaker evidence than a moderate change in a feature present in most samples.</span></span></span> for details.


```{r DA, include=FALSE}
  regex_escape <- function(x) {
    gsub("([+()\\[\\].*?^$|{}\\\\])", "\\\\\\1", x, perl = TRUE)
  }
  .daw <- function(i, default = "70%") {
    w <- imgInfo$daplot_width
    if (!is.null(w) && length(w) >= i && !is.na(w[i])) w[i] else default
  }

  convert_and_include_pdf <- function(tool, index, subgroup = NULL, da_wd, da_com) {
    safe_token <- regex_escape(da_com[index])
    pattern <- sprintf("%s.*\\(%s\\)%s.*\\.pdf$", tool, safe_token, ifelse(is.null(subgroup), "", paste0(".*", subgroup)))
    input_pdf <- list.files(path = da_wd, pattern = pattern, full.names = TRUE)
    
    if(length(input_pdf) == 0) {
      message("No PDF files found for pattern: ", pattern)
      return()
    }
    
    if (length(input_pdf) > 1) {
    
      message("Multiple PDF files matched pattern: ", pattern, " - using the first: ", basename(input_pdf[1]))
    
    }
    
    base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(input_pdf[1]))
    output_png <- file.path(dirname(input_pdf[1]), paste0(base_name, ".png"))
    
    image_read_pdf(input_pdf[1], pages = 1) %>%
      image_convert(format = "png") %>%
      image_write(output_png)
    
    include_graphics(output_png)
  }

# Differential abundance testing (DESeq2, ANCOMBC, ZicoSeq R package) was carried out to determine taxa differences between groups. Here, we identified a small number of bacterial ASVs that differed between the baseline and the other group(s). Significantly differentially abundant bacteria were determined by p < 0.05 (open circle) and padj (FDR) < 0.05 (closed circle) from both tests. For the ZicoSeq plot, random effects were controlled by treating the recorded ID as a longitudinal study. The plot shows padj (FDR) < 0.05 with their intensity of prevalence. The tests are only provided for comparisons that can be performed.
```
